lessons.name: Analytic vs numerical IK shoot-out
lessons.summary: Compare equation-based and iterative inverse kinematics on the same five-joint arm, measuring failures as carefully as speed.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Compare equation-based and iterative inverse kinematics on the same five-joint arm, measuring failures as carefully as speed.

![SO-101 follower arm, a possible five-joint positioning chain for the benchmark](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-ik.webp)
*SO-101 follower arm, a possible five-joint positioning chain for the benchmark. Source: [LeRobot SO-101 docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Inverse kinematics (IK)** turns a desired gripper position and orientation into joint angles; **forward kinematics (FK)** computes the pose from those angles.
- **Analytic IK** solves geometry directly; **numerical IK** repeatedly improves an initial guess. Think of comparing two implementations behind the same API, with identical test fixtures.
- **A degree of freedom** is an independent motion coordinate: five arm joints cannot independently satisfy all six position-and-orientation coordinates.

> **Key idea:** A solver comparison is meaningful only when every method solves the same constrained task.

## What you need

- **Laptop simulation:** Use a laptop, one documented five-joint model, Robotics Toolbox for Python, TRAC-IK, and a geometric solution derived for that particular chain.
- **Starting point:** Finish Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and read Inverse kinematics (analytic & numerical); no physical arm purchase is required.
- **Shared contract:** Specify which orientation components matter, joint limits, pose tolerance, initial guesses, and timeout before collecting results.

## Steps

1. **Validate FK:** Display known joint configurations and confirm the gripper frame and joint order.
2. **Generate reachable targets:** Sample valid joint angles, then compute their poses with FK; save the inputs so every solver receives identical targets.
3. **Implement the adapters:** Return angles, success, elapsed time, and residual, meaning the remaining target error; distinguish unsupported tasks from failed solves.
4. **Run the comparison:** Include repeated seeds, unreachable positions, and targets near joint limits; retain timeout cases.
5. **Check returned angles:** Recompute FK independently and reject limit violations rather than trusting a success flag.
6. **Demo the results:** Replay selected successes and failures beside a table of success rates and solve times.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[Valid angles] --> F[FK targets]
  F --> S[Three solvers]
  S --> V[FK and limit checks]
  V --> T[Benchmark table]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **False fairness:** The Toolbox's general analytic interface targets six-axis arms; do not silently substitute that model for your five-joint derivation.
- **Fast failures:** An immediate rejection is not a fast successful solve; report successful timings and timeout behavior separately.

## When it's done

- **Worked sanity check:** Feed a target generated from a saved configuration back into each solver; different returned angles are acceptable if FK reaches the same permitted pose.
- **Reproducible artifact:** Publish model revision, target set, task constraints, and raw results, including an empty target-set case that produces no misleading averages.

```python
if sol.success:
    verified_pose = robot.fkine(sol.q)
    print(sol.residual)
```

lessons.name: Build a 3D-printed delta picker
lessons.summary: Build a printed parallel robot that transfers small objects, then measure positioning error and completed picks per minute.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Build a printed parallel robot that transfers small objects, then measure positioning error and completed picks per minute.

![Printed delta robot with three branches meeting at a moving platform](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-delta.webp)
*Printed delta robot with three branches meeting at a moving platform. Source: [grzesiek2201/Delta-Robot README](https://github.com/grzesiek2201/Delta-Robot), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A delta robot** joins a fixed platform to a moving platform through three branches; paired passive rods keep the moving platform parallel to the base.
- **Parallel kinematics** means those branches cooperate on one tool position. Unlike separate software workers, they cannot choose mutually inconsistent endpoints.
- **Measured performance** separates commanded coordinates from actual placement, and attempted picks from objects successfully delivered to a tray.

> **Key idea:** Mechanical alignment and calibration matter as much as correct inverse-kinematics code.

## What you need

- **Choose one complete design:** The pictured DIY Delta robot provides models, a parts list, build instructions, and offline visualization; do not mix its dimensions with another build.
- **Hardware access:** Arrange printing, the selected motors and controller, joints, power supply, and a lightweight pickup tool; your local parts cost is unknown.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and study Parallel & closed-chain mechanisms before powering the assembled robot.
- **Published comparison:** Low-cost 3D-printed delta robot (IJMERR 2024) uses three servos, Arduino Uno, and a PCA9685 servo driver; its measurements are not guarantees.

## Steps

1. **Simulate the geometry:** Enter the chosen design's dimensions and test safe reachable points before ordering or printing parts.
2. **Assemble and inspect:** Check branch lengths, free joint movement, and a secure fixed platform; document deviations from the design.
3. **Calibrate the motors:** Establish consistent zero angles and verify each branch independently with small motions.
4. **Add the pickup sequence:** Approach, collect, lift, transfer, and release; treat a missed pickup as a failed cycle.
5. **Measure repeated placements:** Use fixed test locations, record commanded and observed positions, and separate accuracy from repeatability.
6. **Demo the picker:** Transfer small wrapped sweets or similarly lightweight objects while logging completed cycles and elapsed time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Pick location] --> K[IK angles]
  K --> M[Move branches]
  M --> G[Pick and place]
  G --> E[Measure outcomes]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Overclaiming speed:** The IJMERR paper reports 30 picks per minute and 2.2 mm positioning accuracy on its apparatus, not on every printed delta.
- **Mechanical hazard:** Keep fingers clear of moving rods and disconnect motor power before adjusting joints.

## When it's done

- **Worked calculation:** Convert successful transfers divided by elapsed seconds into picks per minute by multiplying by 60; count drops separately.
- **Honest result:** Show repeat trials, failed pickups, placement error, and an unreachable-command rejection, not only the fastest successful video.

```python
picks_per_minute = 60 * successful_transfers / elapsed_seconds
```

lessons.name: CAD-to-sim pipeline for a custom gripper
lessons.summary: Design a gripper assembly in Onshape, export it into MuJoCo, and demonstrate a repeatable simulated cube grasp.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Design a gripper assembly in Onshape, export it into MuJoCo, and demonstrate a repeatable simulated cube grasp.

![Menagerie's Robotiq gripper and hanging cube, a reference setup rather than the proposed custom design](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-gripper.webp)
*Menagerie's Robotiq gripper and hanging cube, a reference setup rather than the proposed custom design. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie Robotiq 2F-85 README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/robotiq_2f85), BSD-2-Clause.*

## What you will learn

- **Computer-aided design (CAD)** describes parts and their assembly; a simulator also needs joints, masses, contact geometry, and actuators, which apply forces or motion commands.
- **The export pipeline** resembles a compiler: the assembly is source code, named mates are declarations, and the exported robot description is a build artifact.
- **A collision shape** is the geometry used for contact calculations; a pretty visual mesh alone does not establish a working grasp.

> **Key idea:** Successful export proves the file can be read, not that its mechanics or contacts are correct.

## What you need

- **Software and access:** Use Onshape, authorized API access, onshape-to-robot, and MuJoCo; simulation requires no printed hardware, while account eligibility and local costs need checking.
- **Preparation:** Revisit Intro: CAD and 3D-print a robot part and Robot description formats (URDF / MJCF).
- **A modest design:** Start with a fixed palm and simple moving fingers; use the pictured Robotiq scene as a contact reference, not as your original CAD.

## Steps

1. **Create the assembly:** Separate rigid links and constrain their intended motion; put the fixed base first in the top-level assembly.
2. **Name the mates:** Use the exporter conventions, including dof_ for movable joints and frame_ for a useful fingertip frame.
3. **Export to MuJoCo:** Set output_format to mujoco in config.json, then inspect the generated robot.xml and scene.xml.
4. **Audit the model:** Check mass, joint axes, travel limits, collisions, and actuator behavior before adding a cube.
5. **Tune the grasp:** Place a cube between open fingers, close slowly, and test whether it stays held during a prescribed movement.
6. **Demo a clean rebuild:** Re-export the same assembly and replay the test with documented initial conditions and failure counts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Onshape assembly] --> X[Export configuration]
  X --> M[MuJoCo model]
  M --> V[Joint and contact checks]
  V --> G[Cube grasp]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Missing declarations:** Unrecognized mates do not become controllable joints; orphaned links can become fixed to the base.
- **Artificial success:** Interpenetrating fingers or excessive contact friction can hide bad geometry; inspect contacts rather than judging only the animation.

## When it's done

- **Worked export check:** A slider named dof_finger becomes a prismatic, or straight-line, joint; a frame_tip becomes a MuJoCo site for inspection.
- **Reproducible delivery:** Save assembly revision, export settings, simulator model, and grasp trials, including a cube placed outside the opening.

```json
{
  "url": "YOUR_ONSHAPE_ASSEMBLY_URL",
  "output_format": "mujoco"
}
```

lessons.name: Camera-to-gripper frame chain on the SO-101
lessons.summary: Project the SO-101 gripper's computed coordinate frame onto a camera image and measure how well the overlay matches reality.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Project the SO-101 gripper's computed coordinate frame onto a camera image and measure how well the overlay matches reality.

![SO-101 follower whose gripper frame will be projected into a camera view](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-frames.webp)
*SO-101 follower whose gripper frame will be projected into a camera view. Source: [LeRobot SO-101 docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A coordinate frame** is an origin plus three directions; the same physical gripper point has different coordinates in the robot base and camera frames.
- **A rigid transform** combines rotation and translation in a 4-by-4 matrix. Chaining transforms is like composing typed functions: adjacent input and output frames must match.
- **Camera intrinsics** describe image formation, including focal lengths and image center; **extrinsics** describe where the camera sits relative to the robot.

> **Key idea:** An overlay tests the entire geometry chain, not just whether an individual matrix looks plausible.

## What you need

- **Starting setup:** Complete Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101, then begin with a simulated arm and camera before testing a fixed real camera.
- **Software:** Use FK, meaning joint angles converted into a gripper pose, plus OpenCV calibration and projection; existing-hardware cost depends on your lab.
- **Map foundations:** Read Rigid-body motion & coordinate frames and Forward kinematics (DH & product of exponentials); record your joint order and units.

## Steps

1. **Define the frames:** Label base, gripper, and camera; write down which direction every stored transform maps.
2. **Calibrate the camera:** Collect a checkerboard from varied views, retaining the image resolution, camera matrix, and lens-distortion coefficients.
3. **Locate the camera:** Estimate its pose relative to a known target attached at a measured pose relative to the robot base.
4. **Compute the chain:** Combine camera-from-base with base-from-gripper FK to express the gripper origin and axis endpoints in camera coordinates.
5. **Project the axes:** Draw those endpoints into the image with the calibrated camera model; compare visible reference points across multiple arm poses.
6. **Demo and measure:** Display the live overlay with per-pose pixel errors and keep the camera fixed during the evaluation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[Joint angles] --> F[Base to gripper FK]
  F --> C[Camera coordinates]
  C --> P[Camera projection]
  P --> O[Overlay and error]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Wrong direction:** OpenCV's solvePnP maps object coordinates into camera coordinates; invert it when your chain requires the opposite direction.
- **Convention mismatch:** OpenCV's camera axes point right, down, and forward; robot model axes need not use that convention.
- **Timing mismatch:** Compare camera frames with corresponding joint readings; moving an arm while pairing unrelated samples can spoil an otherwise correct chain.

## When it's done

- **Worked chain:** Camera-from-base multiplied by base-from-gripper yields camera-from-gripper; reversing the multiplication is not equivalent.
- **Measurable evidence:** Save images, calibration, and pixel-error statistics, including points behind the camera and missing-image handling; hardware stays stationary while checking an uncertain overlay.

```python
T_camera_gripper = T_camera_base @ T_base_gripper
point_camera = T_camera_gripper @ point_gripper
```

lessons.name: Centroidal momentum viewer
lessons.summary: Animate a simulated humanoid with its center of mass and whole-body momentum displayed beside the motion.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Animate a simulated humanoid with its center of mass and whole-body momentum displayed beside the motion.

![Unitree H1 model in MuJoCo Menagerie, a possible humanoid for the viewer](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-momentum.webp)
*Unitree H1 model in MuJoCo Menagerie, a possible humanoid for the viewer. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie Unitree H1 README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/unitree_h1), BSD-3-Clause.*

## What you will learn

- **Center of mass (CoM)** is the mass-weighted average of all body positions; it moves when the robot changes posture, even if the feet remain still.
- **Linear momentum** measures translational motion weighted by mass; **angular momentum** measures rotational motion about a specified point, here the whole-body CoM.
- **Centroidal** means expressed about that center. The viewer is like a debugger showing aggregate state beside the individual objects that produced it.

> **Key idea:** Whole-body momentum compresses many joint motions into a useful summary, but does not certify balance.

## What you need

- **Simulation assets:** Choose a humanoid such as Menagerie's H1, plus Pinocchio and a 3D viewer; no physical humanoid purchase is needed.
- **Consistent model data:** Use matching geometry, masses, joint order, and base conventions for rendering and dynamics; do not silently mix unrelated robot descriptions.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim, then read Floating-base & centroidal dynamics (legged/humanoid).
- **A floating base** is a torso that can translate and rotate instead of being bolted down; include its position and velocity in the state.

## Steps

1. **Load the model:** Display a neutral pose and inspect the total mass and body locations before calculating any overlays.
2. **Supply a motion:** Replay a documented trajectory with positions and velocities, or generate a clearly labeled kinematic animation rather than claiming a balanced controller.
3. **Compute the quantities:** Use Pinocchio's centerOfMass and computeCentroidalMomentum interfaces with the same current state.
4. **Draw separate overlays:** Add a CoM marker and labeled linear and angular momentum vectors, each with its own units and visual scale.
5. **Test the mapping:** Hold the pose fixed while changing velocities; check whether the numerical readout and arrows agree.
6. **Demo the viewer:** Play the humanoid motion with pause, scrub, and numeric readouts so another student can inspect a surprising frame.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Positions and velocities] --> D[CoM and momentum]
  S --> R[Render humanoid]
  D --> O[Labeled overlays]
  R --> O
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Mixed units:** Linear and angular momentum do not share units; a single unlabelled arrow scale makes them misleading.
- **False stability claims:** The CoM marker alone does not describe contacts, actuator limits, or whether a motion can actually execute.

## When it's done

- **Worked check:** With every generalized velocity zero, momentum must be zero even when the bent humanoid's CoM is not at the origin.
- **Repeatable delivery:** Save model revision, motion, vector conventions, and checks for stationary motion, an empty trajectory, and incompatible state dimensions.

```python
com = pin.centerOfMass(model, data, q, v)
momentum = pin.computeCentroidalMomentum(model, data, q, v)
print(com, momentum.linear, momentum.angular)
```

lessons.name: Click-to-reach SO-101
lessons.summary: Turn a camera-image click into a tabletop target for the SO-101, rejecting targets that cannot be reached safely.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Turn a camera-image click into a tabletop target for the SO-101, rejecting targets that cannot be reached safely.

![SO-101 follower arm used for the proposed camera-click reaching interface](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-click.webp)
*SO-101 follower arm used for the proposed camera-click reaching interface. Source: [LeRobot SO-101 docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **An image click** supplies two pixel coordinates, not a full position in space; constrain the exercise to a calibrated tabletop plane rather than guessing depth.
- **Inverse kinematics (IK)** converts the resulting robot-frame target into joint angles; an acceptable position does not imply every gripper orientation is achievable.
- **The interface** resembles a web request pipeline: parse the click, validate coordinates, solve the request, and reject invalid outputs before causing side effects.

> **Key idea:** A click is a request for a checked motion, never permission to send arbitrary joint commands.

## What you need

- **Preparation:** Complete Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101 and Camera-to-gripper frame chain on the SO-101; keep the camera and table fixed.
- **Software:** Use OpenCV calibration, a documented SO-101 model, an IK solver, and a simulator; extra hardware cost depends on existing lab equipment.
- **A restricted task:** Start with reaching above marked tabletop points, not picking objects of unknown height; learn Inverse kinematics (analytic & numerical).

## Steps

1. **Calibrate the scene:** Estimate camera intrinsics, distortion, and table pose from known reference points; retain their physical scale.
2. **Map the click:** Undistort the pixel, form its viewing ray, and intersect that ray with the known table plane.
3. **Transform the target:** Express the intersection in robot-base coordinates and add a deliberately chosen approach clearance.
4. **Solve the reach:** Use position and a feasible orientation constraint; inspect solver success, joint limits, and forward-kinematics error.
5. **Preview before execution:** Check the interpolated path for collisions and limits in simulation, then require explicit confirmation for slow hardware motion.
6. **Demo the interface:** Mark accepted and rejected clicks differently and log target, resulting pose, and reason for each refusal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Pixel click] --> R[Ray meets table]
  R --> B[Robot target]
  B --> I[IK solution]
  I --> V[Path validation]
  V --> A[Confirmed slow reach]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Depth ambiguity:** A pixel over a tall object does not identify its top surface when the interface assumes the tabletop.
- **Endpoint-only checking:** IK does not establish a collision-free route; the elbow can strike the table while the final gripper pose appears valid.
- **Hardware hazard:** Keep the arm's swept volume clear and a motor-power disconnect within reach during confirmed tests.

## When it's done

- **Worked round trip:** Project a known tabletop marker into the image, click its location, and compare the recovered base-frame point with the marker's measured position.
- **Visible failure handling:** Demonstrate normal clicks, unreachable clicks, a ray with no valid forward table intersection, and absent camera frames without moving on invalid input.

```text
Pseudocode with vectors expressed in the same frame:
if abs(dot(normal, ray_direction)) > epsilon:
    distance = dot(normal, plane_point - ray_origin) / dot(normal, ray_direction)
    if distance > 0:
        target = ray_origin + distance * ray_direction
```

lessons.name: Closed-loop leg linkage in MuJoCo
lessons.summary: Export a four-bar leg mechanism into MuJoCo, close its kinematic loop with constraints, and inspect its motion and closure error.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Export a four-bar leg mechanism into MuJoCo, close its kinematic loop with constraints, and inspect its motion and closure error.

![Rhoban's planar closed-chain reference shown cut open into a tree before closure constraints](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-linkage.webp)
*Rhoban's planar closed-chain reference shown cut open into a tree before closure constraints. Source: [Onshape-to-robot Kinematic loops docs](https://onshape-to-robot.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kinematic_loops.html), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **A four-bar linkage** is a loop of rigid links joined by pivots; for this exercise, use one fixed base and moving links that form a simple leg mechanism.
- **A kinematic tree** has one parent per body; closing a mechanical loop requires an additional relationship beyond that tree.
- **An equality constraint** asks the simulator to keep specified points or poses together. Think of a database integrity constraint connecting records stored in separate branches.

> **Key idea:** Cutting a loop makes the model representable as a tree; closure constraints restore the missing mechanical relationship.

## What you need

- **Software:** Use Onshape, authorized API access, onshape-to-robot, and MuJoCo; this project requires no physical leg or printed parts.
- **Preparation:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and study Parallel & closed-chain mechanisms plus Robot description formats (URDF / MJCF).
- **Reference versus deliverable:** Rhoban's pictured planar mechanism explains loop handling; adapt that method to your own four-bar leg rather than calling the reference a four-bar.

## Steps

1. **Design the mechanism:** Define pivot locations, rigid links, and a fixed base; verify its intended movement in CAD before export.
2. **Choose the tree cut:** Add the closing mate with the closing_ prefix so the exporter can identify the missing relationship.
3. **Separate active and passive joints:** Drive the intended input; mark passive joints as not actuated rather than commanding every pivot independently.
4. **Export and inspect:** Select MuJoCo output and check the generated equality elements, joint axes, limits, and initial assembly.
5. **Sweep slowly:** Move through valid input positions while recording the distance between the two cut-side reference points.
6. **Demo the result:** Replay the moving leg beside its input angle and closure-error trace, including positions where motion must stop.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[CAD loop] --> T[Tree and closing mate]
  T --> E[Export equality constraints]
  E --> S[Input joint sweep]
  S --> P[Motion and closure plot]
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Overconstraining:** Actuating passive joints can demand incompatible motions; a numerically jittering mechanism is not evidence of working leg control.
- **Incorrect closure type:** The exporter uses weld for fixed closure, connect for ball closure, and two connect constraints for revolute closure.
- **Ignoring residuals:** Visually overlapping parts can still have constraint error; measure the cut-side points instead of trusting the rendered meshes.

## When it's done

- **Worked configuration:** Set a fixed base with freejoint false and set actuated false for passive joints, matching the documented planar export example.
- **Reproducible package:** Save CAD revision, exported model, sweep inputs, and closure plots; report invalid initial geometry and failed sweeps rather than hiding them.

```json
{
  "output_format": "mujoco",
  "freejoint": false,
  "joint_properties": {"passive_joint": {"actuated": false}}
}
```

lessons.name: Delta robot IK/FK in simulation
lessons.summary: Make a simulated delta robot trace a drawn path, checking analytic inverse kinematics against independently computed numerical forward kinematics.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Make a simulated delta robot trace a drawn path, checking analytic inverse kinematics against independently computed numerical forward kinematics.

![Delta GUI showing a three-arm mechanism and its Cartesian coordinates](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-delta-sim.webp)
*Published Delta GUI with live kinematics; its README also describes offline simulation. Source: [grzesiek2201/Delta-Robot README](https://github.com/grzesiek2201/Delta-Robot), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Parallel mechanism:** Three chains connect a fixed base to a moving platform; their geometry must agree on one platform position.
- **Inverse kinematics (IK)** converts a target position into motor angles; **forward kinematics (FK)** recovers the position from those angles.
- **Round-trip testing:** Think of encoding and decoding a payload using independent implementations; disagreement exposes assumptions that an attractive animation can hide.

> **Key idea:** An IK success flag is not proof of reachability: check joint limits and reconstruct the position independently.

## What you need

- **Laptop setup:** Use Python, NumPy, SciPy, and a plotting window; no hardware purchase is required for this simulation exercise.
- **Geometry contract:** Select one published delta design and record link lengths, platform dimensions, joint limits, coordinate directions, and units together.
- **Starting point:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and read Parallel & closed-chain mechanisms before writing the solvers.

## Steps

1. **Model the chains:** Compute elbow and platform attachment positions; define closure errors as rod-length discrepancies for all three chains.
2. **Implement analytic IK:** Follow the chosen geometry's equations, retaining valid solution branches and rejecting impossible roots or joint-limit violations.
3. **Implement numerical FK:** Minimize closure errors with SciPy, starting from a known platform position; check the final residual and assembly branch.
4. **Round-trip targets:** Feed analytic IK angles into numerical FK; compare reconstructed positions with requested positions, including deliberately unreachable targets.
5. **Draw a path:** Sample a mouse-drawn curve in a fixed-height plane; reject invalid samples visibly rather than connecting them through impossible motion.
6. **Demo the comparison:** Animate valid segments beside requested and reconstructed paths; export errors, branch changes, failures, and timing for each direction separately.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Drawn path] --> I[Analytic IK]
  I --> L[Limit check]
  L --> F[Numerical FK]
  F --> E[Position error]
  E --> V[Replay and report]
```

**Solver sketch:** With `closure_error` from step 1 and `p_seed` on the selected assembly branch, reconstruct one position:

```python
fit = least_squares(lambda p: closure_error(p, q), p_seed)
closure = np.linalg.norm(fit.fun)
position_error = np.linalg.norm(fit.x - target)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Wrong branch:** A small closure error can describe a different assembly configuration; preserve continuity from a known valid pose.
- **Mixed designs:** Do not combine dimensions from one repository with equations assuming different attachment geometry.
- **Invalid samples:** Keep rejected points and solver failures in the results; a successful optimizer termination does not establish a valid robot configuration.

## When it's done

- **Replay artifact:** Another student can redraw a path and see which points are reachable, reconstructed, or rejected.
- **Regression set:** Save fixed targets, declared tolerances, position errors, closure residuals, and separate IK/FK runtimes; report passes and failures without promising hardware accuracy.

lessons.summary: Derive a two-link arm’s torque equations from energy, then compare them with Pinocchio and MuJoCo on identical states.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Derive a two-link arm’s torque equations from energy, then compare them with Pinocchio and MuJoCo on identical states.

![MuJoCo rendering of the hanging Dynamixel 2R testbench arm](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-two-link.webp)
*Dynamixel 2R reference testbench; use a shared idealized two-link fixture for the equation checks. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie Dynamixel 2R README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/dynamixel_2r), MIT License.*

## What you will learn

- **Lagrangian mechanics** turns kinetic energy, from motion, and potential energy, from height, into joint forces or **torques**, meaning turning efforts.
- **Inverse dynamics** predicts the torque needed for specified joint angles, velocities, and accelerations; it does not mean inverse kinematics.
- **Differential testing:** Treat your derivation, Pinocchio, and MuJoCo as three implementations of one function, sharing a serialized robot fixture.

> **Key idea:** Compare instantaneous torque predictions before comparing animations, which also depend on numerical integration and control choices.

## What you need

- **Laptop tools:** Python, NumPy, Pinocchio, MuJoCo, and a notebook for the derivation; no physical arm purchase is required.
- **Shared fixture:** Specify link lengths, masses, centers of mass, rotational inertias, joint axes, zero angles, and gravity in one parameter table.
- **Background:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim, then read Rigid-body dynamics (equations of motion).

## Steps

1. **Draw the coordinates:** Define the two joint angles and each link's center-of-mass position; differentiate those positions to obtain velocities.
2. **Write the energies:** Include translation and rotation for finite rigid links; apply the Lagrange recipe, kinetic energy minus potential energy.
3. **Extract torque terms:** Collect acceleration coefficients into the mass matrix; keep velocity-dependent and gravity terms as a separate bias vector.
4. **Match both models:** Use identical parameters; disable contacts, damping, friction, and **armature**, the added joint inertia, for this idealized comparison.
5. **Compare fixed states:** Test rest, moving joints, nonzero acceleration, and gravity disabled; investigate each disagreement before adding a time integrator.
6. **Demo the evidence:** Present the derivation, per-joint torque residuals, worst-case state, and a reproducible random seed beside the simulated arm.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Shared parameters] --> E[Energy derivation]
  P --> S[Pinocchio and MuJoCo]
  Q[Same state] --> E
  Q --> S
  E --> R[Torque residuals]
  S --> R
```

**Worked comparison:** Once `tau_hand`, `tau_pin`, and `tau_mj` contain predictions for the same state, inspect disagreement in newton-meters:

```python
pin_error = np.max(np.abs(tau_hand - tau_pin))
mj_error = np.max(np.abs(tau_hand - tau_mj))
print(pin_error, mj_error)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Different bodies:** A point-mass derivation cannot match a finite-inertia model unless you explicitly reconcile their assumptions.
- **Gravity signs:** A different angle origin or gravity direction can reverse the expected holding torque.
- **Actuator confusion:** Compare required generalized forces from inverse dynamics, not position-controller commands or contact forces.

## When it's done

- **Numerical agreement:** All three implementations agree within an explicitly justified floating-point tolerance; report maximum absolute and relative errors, handling zero torques separately.
- **Diagnostic tests:** Mass-matrix symmetry, gravity-at-rest checks, and saved failing inputs make the derivation maintainable when parameters change.

lessons.name: Diff-drive odometry from scratch
lessons.summary: Estimate a simulated two-wheel robot’s path from wheel rotations, overlay ground truth, and explain why the estimate drifts.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Estimate a simulated two-wheel robot’s path from wheel rotations, overlay ground truth, and explain why the estimate drifts.

![Published two-wheel robot CAD model with independently driven wheels](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-odometry.webp)
*Two-wheel reference robot from the Onshape-to-robot examples; the exercise estimates this kind of base motion. Source: [Onshape-to-robot examples README](https://github.com/Rhoban/onshape-to-robot-examples), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Differential drive** steers by driving left and right wheels at different speeds; the robot cannot slide sideways in the ideal rolling model.
- **Odometry** accumulates small movements inferred from wheel rotations; **ground truth** is the simulator's actual pose, kept outside the estimator.
- **Stateful integration:** Like replaying an event log, every wheel increment updates the previous estimate, including any earlier error.

> **Key idea:** A correct wheel-motion integrator can still drift when its wheel dimensions or no-slip assumptions are wrong.

## What you need

- **Laptop experiment:** Python, NumPy, plotting, and a simulated differential-drive base; no hardware purchase or ROS installation is required.
- **Geometry:** Record left and right wheel radii, wheel separation, rotation signs, starting pose, and sample timestamps.
- **Background:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim, then read Wheeled mobile robot kinematics and Wheel & inertial dead reckoning.

## Steps

1. **Generate measurements:** Log simulated wheel angles and independent chassis poses for straight motion, in-place turns, and a square route.
2. **Convert increments:** Multiply each wheel's angular change by its radius; average the traveled distances for forward motion and divide their difference by separation for heading.
3. **Integrate the pose:** Implement constant-curvature arc updates, including the straight-line limit; rotate local displacement into the world using the previous heading.
4. **Check ideal motion:** Replay logs without reading truth inside the estimator; verify equal increments drive straight and opposite increments turn in place.
5. **Inject mismatch:** Change one assumed wheel radius, then introduce simulated slip separately; plot each estimate against unchanged ground truth.
6. **Demo drift:** Animate the square, report final position and heading errors, and compare errors over distance rather than showing only the endpoint.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[Wheel readings] --> D[Distance increments]
  D --> U[Pose update]
  U --> U
  U --> P[Overlay paths]
  G[Simulator truth] --> P
```

**Worked increment:** For radii `r_left`, `r_right`, wheel changes in radians, and separation `track` in meters:

```python
dl = r_left * delta_left
dr = r_right * delta_right
ds = (dr + dl) / 2
dtheta = (dr - dl) / track
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Command leakage:** Integrating requested speeds hides actuator and contact effects; use measured wheel changes for the estimator.
- **Angle wrapping:** Unwrap encoder readings before differencing and compare headings modulo a full turn.
- **False cancellation:** A route may finish near its start despite substantial intermediate error; inspect the entire trace.

## When it's done

- **Replayable result:** Save wheel logs, truth, estimator parameters, and the overlay plot; rerunning the estimator must not require the simulator.
- **Failure accounting:** Test stationary input, straight motion, turns, and bad timestamps; explain which drift comes from integration versus incorrect geometry or slip.

lessons.name: FK accuracy check against a camera
lessons.summary: Compare SO-101 forward-kinematics predictions with camera-measured marker positions and map the disagreement across the workspace.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Compare SO-101 forward-kinematics predictions with camera-measured marker positions and map the disagreement across the workspace.

![SO-101 MuJoCo model with yellow links and a camera mount](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-camera-fk.webp)
*Published SO-101 model, the prediction side of the experiment; the measured side needs a real camera and mounted marker. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie SO101 README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/robotstudio_so101), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **Forward kinematics (FK)** predicts tool position and orientation from joint angles and link geometry; a camera provides a separate measurement route.
- **Fiducial marker:** A printed square with identifiable corners lets calibrated-camera software estimate its position and orientation relative to the camera.
- **Independent oracle:** Think of checking a function against externally measured fixtures, not against output generated by that same function.

> **Key idea:** A camera-versus-model discrepancy includes measurement and registration error; it is not automatically a bad link length.

## What you need

- **Hardware setup:** An assembled SO-101, fixed webcam, printed ArUco marker, calibration board, and rigid marker mount; purchase costs depend on existing equipment.
- **Software setup:** Python, OpenCV, a matching FK model, timestamped joint readings, and saved camera calibration at the recording resolution.
- **Prerequisites:** Finish Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101; review Forward kinematics (DH & product of exponentials) and Kinematic & hand-eye calibration.

## Steps

1. **Calibrate the camera:** Estimate its internal projection parameters and lens distortion; measure the printed marker side length rather than assuming printer scale.
2. **Register the frames:** Establish camera-to-base and tool-to-marker transforms independently; keep registration poses separate from evaluation poses.
3. **Validate in simulation:** Generate known marker poses and projected corners; verify transform direction, units, and corner ordering before collecting physical data.
4. **Collect stationary samples:** Move slowly through visible workspace poses, stop, and record joint angles, marker corners, images, timestamps, and detection failures.
5. **Compare marker positions:** Predict the marker through tool FK; transform the camera's marker estimate into the same base frame, then compute their displacement.
6. **Demo the error map:** Plot predicted positions colored by displacement magnitude; include repeated samples at fixed poses and report visibility-related exclusions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[Joint angles] --> F[FK and marker offset]
  I[Camera image] --> M[Marker pose]
  M --> B[Camera to base]
  F --> E[Compare positions]
  B --> E
  E --> V[Workspace error map]
```

**Worked comparison:** Here `T_base_marker_fk` and `T_base_marker_camera` both map marker coordinates into base coordinates; translation entries are in meters:

```python
delta = T_base_marker_fk[:3, 3] - T_base_marker_camera[:3, 3]
error_mm = 1000 * np.linalg.norm(delta)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Wrong direction:** OpenCV's PnP output maps object coordinates into the camera frame, not the reverse.
- **Circular validation:** Registering the camera using every evaluation pose can absorb the very model errors you want to measure.
- **False certainty:** Repeat stationary observations to estimate camera scatter; retain missing or ambiguous detections instead of silently assigning zero error.

> **Watch out:** Keep hands and camera cables outside the powered arm's reachable area.

## When it's done

- **Evidence package:** Save raw observations, frame definitions, registration data, predicted/measured positions, and a workspace plot with median, maximum, and repeatability statistics.
- **Honest scope:** Report the measured disagreement and missing detections without claiming a camera noise floor or an SO-101 accuracy specification you have not established.

lessons.name: Follow a moving target with mink
lessons.summary: Make a MuJoCo arm follow a mouse-dragged target using mink while keeping joint, velocity, and selected collision limits active.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Make a MuJoCo arm follow a mouse-dragged target using mink while keeping joint, velocity, and selected collision limits active.

![mink UR5e example comparing collision avoidance with a red unconstrained arm intersecting a wall](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-mink.webp)
*mink UR5e collision-avoidance example; the red overlay shows motion without avoidance. Source: [mink README](https://github.com/kevinzakka/mink), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **Differential inverse kinematics** computes a small joint-velocity update that reduces the difference between the current tool pose and a target pose.
- **Task versus limit:** A task requests motion; a limit restricts allowed motion. mink combines them in a **quadratic program**, an optimization with quadratic cost.
- **Update loop:** Think of a game loop that reads the dragged target, solves for a legal velocity, integrates it, and redraws the arm.

> **Key idea:** An unreachable target should produce visible tracking error, not permission to violate a joint or collision limit.

## What you need

- **Laptop setup:** MuJoCo, mink, its example dependencies, and a supported optimization solver; no physical arm purchase is required.
- **Reference example:** Start with mink's UR5e collision-avoidance example and its scene rather than assembling unrelated robot and obstacle files.
- **Background:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim; read Differential IK & redundancy resolution (QP-based).

## Steps

1. **Run the example:** Load the home pose and locate the target body; use MuJoCo's interactive viewer to move it with the mouse.
2. **Inspect objectives:** Identify the end-effector frame task and posture task; the latter favors a reference joint configuration while the former tracks the target.
3. **Audit the limits:** Retain configuration and velocity limits; inspect the explicit geometry pairs used by the collision-avoidance limit.
4. **Instrument the loop:** Record pose error, joint positions, joint velocities, solver status, and separation for every protected geometry pair at each update.
5. **Exercise difficult targets:** Drag slowly toward a joint boundary, through the wall, and beyond reach; retain errors and handle solver failures without integrating invalid output.
6. **Demo legal tracking:** Replay reachable and blocked targets with live error and limit indicators; explain which obstacle pairs are protected and which remain unchecked.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[Mouse target] --> T[Task error]
  T --> Q[QP solve with limits]
  Q --> I[Integrate joints]
  I --> T
  I --> V[Viewer and diagnostics]
```

**Core update:** After configuring tasks and limits, use the same timestep for solving and integration:

```python
velocity = mink.solve_ik(configuration, tasks, dt, solver, limits=limits)
configuration.integrate_inplace(velocity, dt)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Partial protection:** The example protects specified wrist-to-environment geometry pairs; that does not imply whole-arm self-collision avoidance.
- **Excessive steps:** Local, linearized limits do not replace checking the resulting configuration and distances after integration.
- **Wrong promise:** This example updates configurations kinematically; it does not demonstrate a torque controller tracking the motion under physical loads.

## When it's done

- **Interactive result:** Reachable mouse targets track, blocked ones leave visible error, and the logged joint ranges and protected separations respect your declared tolerances.
- **Reproducible failures:** Save the scene, target replay, timestep, limits, solver settings, and failure counts so another student can rerun the stress cases.

lessons.summary: Implement SO-101 forward kinematics with Denavit–Hartenberg parameters, products of exponentials, and MuJoCo, then compare their predicted tool poses.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Implement SO-101 forward kinematics with Denavit–Hartenberg parameters, products of exponentials, and MuJoCo, then compare their predicted tool poses.

![Published SO-101 MuJoCo model with yellow links extending horizontally](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-fk-three.webp)
*SO-101 reference model; all three implementations must describe the same base, joints, and tool frame. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie SO101 README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/robotstudio_so101), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **Forward kinematics (FK)** maps joint angles to a tool's position and orientation; a **transform** packages that pose into a matrix.
- **Denavit–Hartenberg (DH)** represents a joint chain with link-frame parameters; **product of exponentials (PoE)** composes motions around joint axes from a reference configuration.
- **Interoperability test:** Think of three serializers for the same object; agreement requires identical units, field order, and frame definitions, not identical internal representations.

> **Key idea:** Agreement between three implementations validates your geometry conversion, not the accuracy of that geometry on a physical arm.

## What you need

- **Laptop tools:** Python, NumPy, Robotics Toolbox for Python, MuJoCo, and one pinned SO-101 model; no hardware purchase is required.
- **Shared contract:** Record the base frame, tool frame, joint order, positive directions, angle offsets, and fixed gripper opening.
- **Starting point:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and read Forward kinematics (DH & product of exponentials).

## Steps

1. **Inspect the reference:** Load the SO-101 model, identify its moving joints, and add a named tool site at the agreed measurement point.
2. **Build the DH table:** Assign link frames using one DH convention; include joint offsets and constant base/tool transforms rather than patching individual test poses.
3. **Build the PoE chain:** Extract each joint axis at the reference pose and the reference tool transform; express all axes in one documented frame.
4. **Create a MuJoCo adapter:** Set joint positions, run forward computation, and read the named site's world pose; convert it to the agreed base frame.
5. **Compare shared inputs:** Test the reference pose, one moving joint at a time, and seeded random poses inside limits; measure position and orientation separately.
6. **Demo discrepancies:** Overlay predicted tool frames, export pairwise errors, and retain the worst pose for debugging rather than showing only matching examples.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q[Shared joint vector] --> D[DH chain]
  Q --> P[PoE chain]
  Q --> M[MuJoCo FK]
  D --> E[Pairwise pose errors]
  P --> E
  M --> E
```

**Worked position check:** After normalizing frames, this computes one pair's tool-origin distance in meters; repeat for the other two pairs:

```python
error = np.linalg.norm(T_dh[:3, 3] - T_poe[:3, 3])
assert error < 0.001
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Mixed conventions:** Standard DH and modified DH are different parameterizations; do not mix their link transforms.
- **Frame mismatch:** A mesh origin, wrist frame, and tool tip are not interchangeable measurement points.
- **Angle shortcuts:** Compare rotation matrices through a relative rotation, not by subtracting Euler angles near wrap boundaries.

## When it's done

- **Position target:** Every pair agrees within the project's chosen one-millimeter threshold on the saved random-pose set; report the maximum error, not just the average.
- **Orientation target:** Declare a separate angular tolerance, report results in radians, and save model revision, parameter tables, transforms, seeds, and failing inputs.

lessons.name: Full inertial identification of the SO-101
lessons.summary: Estimate physically consistent SO-101 link inertias from recorded motion and torque data, then evaluate torque predictions on motions excluded from fitting.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Estimate physically consistent SO-101 link inertias from recorded motion and torque data, then evaluate torque predictions on motions excluded from fitting.

![SO-101 model with multiple articulated yellow links shown in MuJoCo](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-inertia.webp)
*SO-101 reference model for the simulated identification stage, before any claims about a real arm. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie SO101 README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/robotstudio_so101), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **Inertial parameters** describe mass, center of mass, and resistance to angular acceleration; they connect motion with required **torque**, or turning effort.
- **Identification** estimates model parameters from observations; **excitation trajectories** deliberately vary motion so the data reveal more than a static holding pose.
- **Train/test split:** Like machine learning, lower training error is unconvincing unless predictions improve on separate motions.

> **Key idea:** Some link parameters are observable only in combinations; physically plausible fitted inertias need not be the uniquely correct inertias.

## What you need

- **Simulation baseline:** Python, Pinocchio, a consistent SO-101 description, and a constrained optimizer; start without purchasing hardware.
- **Real-data gate:** Hardware requires synchronized joint states and calibrated torque measurements or estimates; servo commands are not measured torque.
- **Background:** Finish STS3215 actuator model for sim-to-real; review Dynamic parameter identification & actuator models and Efficient dynamics algorithms & analytical derivatives.

## Steps

1. **Validate the pipeline:** Generate simulated motion and torques from known parameters; perturb the initial model and reserve evaluation trajectories.
2. **Design excitation:** Vary joint positions, velocities, and accelerations within limits; timestamp observations and inspect distinguishable parameter combinations.
3. **Prepare observations:** Align signals, estimate derivatives, document filtering, and handle boundary artifacts; fit friction separately rather than hiding it in link masses.
4. **Fit constrained parameters:** Build the torque regressor, the matrix linking inertial parameters to torques; enforce physical-consistency constraints, including realizable inertia and positive masses.
5. **Validate held-out motions:** Compare baseline and identified torque predictions; report per-joint errors, residuals, exclusions, and unidentifiable combinations.
6. **Demo the result:** Replay predicted torques; collect real-arm data only after validating sensing and actuator models, then repeat held-out evaluation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E[Excitation motions] --> L[Aligned state and torque logs]
  L --> F[Physically constrained fit]
  F --> P[Identified parameters]
  P --> V[Held-out torque prediction]
  B[Baseline parameters] --> V
```

**Worked score:** With held-out predicted and measured torques shaped as samples by joints, compute per-joint root-mean-square error in newton-meters:

```python
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((tau_pred - tau_measured)**2, axis=0))
print(rmse)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Servo mismatch:** BAM documents extended friction models, including STS3215 support; friction or drive errors must not be mistaken for changed link inertia.
- **Unphysical solutions:** Low unconstrained least-squares error does not prove the resulting masses and inertias describe a realizable body.
- **Data leakage:** Splitting neighboring samples from one filtered trajectory is weaker than holding out complete motions; record the split before fitting.

> **Watch out:** Keep people outside the powered arm's reach during any excitation experiment and retain an immediate stop mechanism.

## When it's done

- **Deliverable:** Export physically consistent link parameters, frame conventions, held-out torque errors before/after fitting, and the reproducible experiment.
- **Honest boundaries:** Report torque calibration, parameters constrained by prior assumptions, and whether improvements survive held-out motions; reject empty evaluation logs.

lessons.summary: Train a simulated pushing policy through contact gradients and compare it with PPO on the same held-out object-and-goal trials.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Train a simulated pushing policy through contact gradients and compare it with PPO on the same held-out object-and-goal trials.

![Published Panda reference arm; add the object and goal for this proposed pushing experiment](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-push.webp)
*Published Panda reference arm; add the object and goal for this proposed pushing experiment. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie Panda README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/franka_emika_panda), Apache-2.0 License.*

## What you will learn

- **Policy:** A function maps observations, such as object and goal positions, to arm commands; its parameters determine the pushing behavior.
- **Differentiable simulation** supplies derivatives of outcomes with respect to inputs, letting an optimizer propagate task error backward through a simulated rollout.
- **Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)** learns a policy from sampled interactions; its policy gradients do not require derivatives through the physics simulator.
- **Software analogy:** Backpropagation through a physics rollout resembles training a recurrent network, but contact can make its gradients misleading or uninformative.

> **Key idea:** Fast simulation and useful contact gradients are different capabilities; validate both before comparing learning algorithms.

## What you need

- **Simulation setup:** Use Python, JAX, public MJX-JAX, and a Panda arm with a tabletop object; no physical robot purchase is required.
- **DiffMJX access:** Its setup requires private component repositories; verify access before choosing it, or study public MJX-JAX while documenting its contact-gradient limitations.
- **Comparison setup:** Give both learners identical observations, actions, rewards, resets, and evaluation trials; record compute requirements.
- **Background:** Finish Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim; read Contact dynamics & differentiable simulation and inspect DiffMJX.

## Steps

1. **Define the task:** Push one object toward a goal; declare success distance, time limit, joint bounds, and collision failures before training.
2. **Validate rollouts:** Test object motion with and without contact; keep forward simulation identical for both learners.
3. **Probe gradients:** Compare derivatives with finite perturbations away from contact switches; inspect zero gradients before contact and sensitivity near impact.
4. **Train the policy:** Differentiate a short rollout loss; record gradient norms, failures, compilation time, and training time.
5. **Train PPO:** Use the same task contract; report environment interactions and wall-clock cost separately.
6. **Demo held-out trials:** Replay saved starts and goals, including unreachable goals; report failures, final distances, and multiple training seeds.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Observation] --> P[Policy]
  P --> S[Contact simulation]
  S --> L[Goal loss]
  L --> G[Backward gradients]
  G --> P
  S --> O
```

**Worked loss:** With object and goal positions in meters, score squared distance using differentiable JAX operations:

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp
loss = jnp.sum((object_position - goal_position)**2)
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Backend confusion:** MuJoCo Warp's README says differentiability via Warp is not yet available; GPU acceleration alone does not satisfy the gradient requirement.
- **Biased gradients:** DiffMJX addresses contact-gradient problems, but a successful backward pass is not proof of accurate derivatives in your scene.
- **Empty evaluation:** Reject an empty trial set instead of reporting a success percentage or hiding unstable rollouts.

## When it's done

- **Evidence:** Save scene revisions, training settings, trial seeds, learning curves, and paired evaluation videos; label this a student experiment, not an established DiffMJX pushing result.

lessons.summary: Optimize a simulated arm’s throwing trajectory using Pinocchio derivatives, then test whether the released ball reaches a cup.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Optimize a simulated arm’s throwing trajectory using Pinocchio derivatives, then test whether the released ball reaches a cup.

![Published Panda reference model, before adding a ball, release event, and cup](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-throw-sim.webp)
*Published Panda reference model, before adding a ball, release event, and cup. Source: [MuJoCo Menagerie Panda README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco_menagerie/tree/main/franka_emika_panda), Apache-2.0 License.*

## What you will learn

- **Trajectory optimization** chooses an entire motion rather than one target pose; position, velocity, acceleration, and release timing all affect a throw.
- **Analytical derivatives** describe how predicted dynamics change when inputs change, giving an optimizer local guidance without perturbing every variable separately.
- **Software analogy:** Treat the trajectory as a parameterized program and the landing error as its test loss; derivatives guide parameter updates.

> **Key idea:** Reaching a release position is insufficient: the ball also needs the correct release velocity and a feasible arm motion.

## What you need

- **Laptop tools:** Pinocchio, NumPy, SciPy, MuJoCo, and matching Panda models; this simulation exercise requires no hardware purchase.
- **Scene contract:** Specify cup geometry, ball size, gravity, release rule, and joint, speed, and torque limits; record the assumptions used before and after release.
- **Background:** Read Efficient dynamics algorithms & analytical derivatives and Trajectory generation & time scaling after Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim.

## Steps

1. **Build a release test:** Carry the ball with the tool until a declared release event; verify its initial free-flight position and velocity independently.
2. **Parameterize motion:** Choose smooth joint curves and a release time; compute their joint positions, velocities, accelerations, and inverse-dynamics torques.
3. **Define the objective:** Penalize cup-plane landing error and excessive effort; impose explicit motion bounds rather than assuming a low cost guarantees feasibility.
4. **Supply derivatives:** Combine Pinocchio dynamics derivatives with trajectory and landing-model derivatives; compare selected components against finite differences before optimizing.
5. **Optimize and replay:** Try multiple initial guesses, then simulate the complete throw; retain failed solves and inspect constraint violations between sampled trajectory points.
6. **Demo the result:** Show optimized versus initial trajectories, predicted versus simulated landing points, and sensitivity to release-time perturbations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Trajectory parameters] --> D[Arm dynamics]
  D --> R[Release state]
  R --> B[Ball flight]
  B --> E[Landing error]
  E --> G[Derivative update]
  G --> P
```

**Worked flight check:** Ignoring drag after release, `position = release_position + release_velocity*t + 0.5*gravity*t*t`; use the positive crossing time of the cup-opening plane.

## Common pitfalls

- **Missing chain rule:** Pinocchio derivatives cover robot dynamics, not automatically your spline, gripper release, or ball-flight objective.
- **Cup-plane ambiguity:** Distinguish passing through the opening from hitting its rim or bouncing out; report the chosen success definition.
- **Impossible targets:** Keep unreachable throws and empty target sets as explicit outcomes, not misleading averages.

## When it's done

- **Reproducible artifact:** Save models, optimizer settings, initial guesses, trajectory samples, release states, landing residuals, and a replay with all declared bounds checked.

lessons.name: Gravity-compensated SO-101 'floating arm'
lessons.summary: Build model-based gravity compensation for an SO-101, validating the actuator interface before testing compliant hand-guiding.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Build model-based gravity compensation for an SO-101, validating the actuator interface before testing compliant hand-guiding.

![SO-101 follower reference arm; its pictured pose does not demonstrate a validated floating mode](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-floating.webp)
*SO-101 follower reference arm; its pictured pose does not demonstrate a validated floating mode. Source: [TheRobotStudio SO-ARM100/SO-101 README](https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **Gravity compensation** supplies joint **torques**, or turning efforts, to oppose weight; unlike position holding, its goal is not to return to one fixed configuration.
- **Compliance** means yielding under external force; friction, damping, model error, and the servo's internal controller affect whether hand-guiding feels smooth.
- **Software analogy:** The dynamics model produces a desired torque, but a hardware adapter must translate that request into a command the actuator actually supports.

> **Key idea:** Computing gravity torque does not create torque-control support in a position-controlled servo.

## What you need

- **Simulation first:** Python, Pinocchio, MuJoCo, and an SO-101 description; model validation can start without buying hardware.
- **Hardware stage:** An assembled arm, documented servo configuration, calibrated command mapping, logging, and a stop mechanism; costs depend on existing equipment.
- **Prerequisites:** Finish Assemble & teleoperate an SO-101; review Rigid-body dynamics (equations of motion) and Dynamic parameter identification & actuator models.

## Steps

1. **Audit servo support:** Check the exact motor and firmware command modes; stock STS3215 position control must not be presented as closed-loop torque control.
2. **Validate gravity predictions:** Compare Pinocchio and simulator holding torques at stationary poses, with consistent masses, gravity direction, angle signs, and payload assumptions.
3. **Demonstrate simulated support:** Apply gravity feedforward with damping and limits; compare sag, drift, and response to a brief external perturbation against compensation disabled.
4. **Build the adapter:** For position-controlled hardware, investigate a calibrated position-offset approach; bound offsets and test one supported joint before enabling the chain.
5. **Instrument failure handling:** Log state age, commanded offsets, velocities, saturation, and communication failures; reject stale readings and restore a tested safe mode.
6. **Demo guiding:** At validated settings, show gentle repositioning and release at several poses; report residual drift and cases that cannot be made compliant.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q[Measured joints] --> G[Gravity model]
  G --> A[Validated actuator adapter]
  A --> L[Limits and watchdog]
  L --> R[Arm]
  R --> Q
```

**Worked model call:** `tau_g = pin.computeGeneralizedGravity(model, data, q)` returns generalized gravity forces; a revolute joint's component is torque, not a servo position command.

## Common pitfalls

- **Unvalidated port:** Pollen's SO-100 example computes and visualizes gravity torques; it is not proof that your SO-101 safely floats.
- **Friction masking:** A joint staying still can indicate gearbox friction rather than correct compensation; test approach directions and perturbations.
- **Unsafe fallback:** Disabling motor effort can let the arm fall; establish the failure response before hand contact.

> **Watch out:** Support the arm during initial enabling and keep fingers outside joints and pinch points.

## When it's done

- **Evidence:** Save interface capability checks, calibration, supported poses, drift logs, and a guiding video; clearly separate simulation results from validated hardware behavior.

lessons.name: Hand-eye calibration in sim
lessons.summary: Recover a simulated wrist camera’s transform from robot poses and tag observations, then compare it with hidden simulator ground truth.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Recover a simulated wrist camera’s transform from robot poses and tag observations, then compare it with hidden simulator ground truth.

![OpenCV eye-in-hand diagram showing base, gripper, camera, and stationary target frames](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-hand-eye.webp)
*OpenCV eye-in-hand diagram showing base, gripper, camera, and stationary target frames. Source: [OpenCV Camera Calibration and 3D Reconstruction docs](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Hand-eye calibration** estimates the fixed camera-to-gripper transform; moving the arm changes the camera view without changing that mounting transform.
- **Observability** asks whether the collected motions contain enough information to determine the unknown transform; repeated similar poses can leave directions poorly constrained.
- **Software analogy:** Generate synthetic fixtures with known answers, hide those answers from the solver, and check the recovered result independently.

> **Key idea:** Diverse rotations reveal mounting geometry that many nearly identical views cannot identify reliably.

## What you need

- **Laptop setup:** MuJoCo, Python, NumPy, and OpenCV; no physical camera purchase is required for this synthetic experiment.
- **Scene:** Attach a camera rigidly to a simulated gripper and place a stationary fiducial target within view; record image size and camera projection parameters.
- **Background:** Complete Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim; read Kinematic & hand-eye calibration and Extrinsic & multi-sensor calibration.

## Steps

1. **Hide ground truth:** Save the true camera mounting transform for evaluation only; render tag views and record gripper-to-base poses at matching timestamps.
2. **Recover tag poses:** Detect corners and estimate target-to-camera transforms using known target dimensions; exclude failed detections with explicit reasons.
3. **Collect diverse motions:** Include rotations about different axes; repeat with nearly identical poses to construct a deliberately weak dataset.
4. **Solve calibration:** Pass gripper-to-base and target-to-camera rotations and translations to OpenCV; its output maps camera coordinates into the gripper frame.
5. **Evaluate recovery:** Compare translation and relative rotation with hidden truth; inject corner noise and repeat trials for both pose collections.
6. **Demo the contrast:** Replay views beside mounting-error distributions; validate on held-out images rather than fitting and scoring the same observations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Robot poses] --> C[Calibration]
  I[Rendered corners] --> T[Target poses]
  T --> C
  C --> E[Hidden-truth comparison]
  G[True mounting] --> E
```

**Worked API call:** `R, t = cv2.calibrateHandEye(R_gripper2base, t_gripper2base, R_target2cam, t_target2cam)` returns camera-to-gripper rotation and translation; keep all translations in one unit.

## Common pitfalls

- **Insufficient motion:** OpenCV requires at least three poses with two nonparallel rotation axes; collecting many more views is recommended.
- **Circular validation:** Reading the simulator's camera pose into the calibration inputs bypasses the image-based problem.
- **Empty detections:** Stop with a clear diagnostic when no usable pose pairs remain; do not produce a nominal identity transform.

## When it's done

- **Artifact:** Save images, synchronized pose pairs, camera parameters, noise settings, recovered transforms, and separate translation/angular errors for diverse and degenerate motion sets.

lessons.name: Humanoid jump with Crocoddyl
lessons.summary: Plan a simulated humanoid jump with Crocoddyl and test the motion in MuJoCo without hiding tracking or landing failures.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Plan a simulated humanoid jump with Crocoddyl and test the motion in MuJoCo without hiding tracking or landing failures.

![Published Crocoddyl dynamic maneuvers, including a humanoid jumping between supports](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-jump.webp)
*Published Crocoddyl dynamic maneuvers, including a humanoid jumping between supports. Source: [Carlos Mastalli Crocoddyl publication page](https://cmastalli.github.io/publications/crocoddyl20icra.html), license unknown.*

## What you will learn

- **Optimal control** chooses motion and joint **torques**, or turning efforts, to reduce a cost under a dynamics model and chosen contact phases.
- **Floating base:** A humanoid's torso moves freely; its joints cannot directly command base motion, which depends on gravity and contact forces.
- **Software analogy:** A planner produces a candidate execution trace; replaying it in a separate simulator is an integration test, not merely an animation.

> **Key idea:** A feasible planned contact sequence does not guarantee that a different simulator or tracking controller will reproduce it.

## What you need

- **Simulation tools:** Crocoddyl, Pinocchio, MuJoCo, plotting, and matching humanoid descriptions; no physical humanoid purchase is needed.
- **Model contract:** Match masses, inertias, joints, initial state, feet, ground, and actuator bounds; document state ordering and floating-base orientation conventions.
- **Background:** Finish Intro: robot anatomy & coordinate frames in sim and read Floating-base & centroidal dynamics (legged/humanoid).

## Steps

1. **Inspect the example:** Read Crocoddyl's biped jumping-problem builder; identify supported takeoff, unsupported flight, foot switching, and supported landing phases.
2. **Start modestly:** Solve a small proposed jump from a stable stance; declare target displacement, phase durations, effort limits, and landing requirements.
3. **Audit the plan:** Plot joint states, torques, contact forces, and solver convergence; verify constraints explicitly rather than treating penalties as hard guarantees.
4. **Map the state:** Convert joint order, base position, quaternion convention, velocities, and control units into the MuJoCo model; first validate a stationary stance.
5. **Replay dynamically:** Track the trajectory using bounded controls and documented feedback; distinguish this rollout from directly setting the planned joint positions.
6. **Demo and perturb:** Show takeoff, flight, and landing, then vary initial state or contact settings; retain falls and explain planner-versus-replay discrepancies.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Contact phases] --> O[Crocoddyl solve]
  O --> A[Plan audit]
  A --> M[State and control mapping]
  M --> R[MuJoCo rollout]
  R --> E[Landing metrics]
```

**Worked metric:** `landing_error = np.linalg.norm(actual_foot_position - target_foot_position)` measures one foot's landing displacement; separately record base stability, slip, and actuator saturation.

## Common pitfalls

- **Reference-only success:** A moving visualization does not prove the simulated robot generated the necessary ground reaction forces.
- **Contact mismatch:** Crocoddyl's prescribed support phases and MuJoCo's contact resolution are different modeling choices; report both.
- **Missing trials:** Reject empty replay sets and count solver failures and falls instead of averaging only successful landings.

## When it's done

- **Evidence:** Save model revisions, phase schedule, solver logs, mapping code, control settings, and side-by-side planned/dynamic replay with measured landing errors.

lessons.name: Identified-model dynamic throw on the real SO-101
lessons.summary: Use an identified SO-101 model to plan light-ball throws, then compare predicted and measured landing points at three chosen distances.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Use an identified SO-101 model to plan light-ball throws, then compare predicted and measured landing points at three chosen distances.

![SO-101 follower reference hardware; this photograph is not a demonstrated throwing result](/img/lessons/projects_kinematics_dynamics_1-throw-real.webp)
*SO-101 follower reference hardware; this photograph is not a demonstrated throwing result. Source: [TheRobotStudio SO-ARM100/SO-101 README](https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100), Apache License 2.0.*

## What you will learn

- **System identification** estimates dynamics from measured behavior; a useful throwing model must include actuator response, not just rigid-link inertias.
- **Feedforward** anticipates the command needed for a planned motion; feedback corrects observed errors, subject to communication delays and actuator limits.
- **Software analogy:** Simulation is a staging environment; hardware trials reveal integration errors that a perfectly matching synthetic test cannot expose.

> **Key idea:** A feasible throw still needs measured limits, repeatable release timing, and a calibrated mapping from torque (turning effort) to servo commands.

## What you need

- **Prerequisites:** Complete Full inertial identification of the SO-101, Gradient-based trajectory optimization of a throw, and Model-based torque feedforward on the SO-101.
- **Bench setup:** An assembled arm, very light foam ball, enclosed landing area, bins, camera, synchronized logs, and an immediate stop; costs depend on existing equipment.
- **Validated model:** Keep identified inertial and actuator parameters, uncertainty, command limits, and communication timing; do not replace measured capabilities with nominal stall ratings.

## Steps

1. **Validate slow tracking:** Reproduce held-out motions without releasing anything; compare measured joints with predictions and stop if the actuator adapter saturates or behaves unexpectedly.
2. **Calibrate release:** Measure delay between opening commands and ball departure; keep ball placement and gripper opening consistent across trials.
3. **Plan in simulation:** Optimize within validated speed, command, and predicted torque limits; include release-delay uncertainty and reject infeasible target distances.
4. **Execute conservatively:** Begin with the shortest feasible throw inside containment; log joints, commands, timestamps, predicted release state, and observed ball departure.
5. **Measure and refine:** Compare predicted and measured landing points; distinguish tracking, release, and flight-model errors before changing model parameters.
6. **Demo three distances:** Film repeated throws into bins at three declared feasible distances; hold back evaluation trials after refinement and retain every miss.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[Identified model] --> P[Constrained plan]
  P --> A[Validated command adapter]
  A --> T[Contained throw]
  T --> E[Landing and tracking errors]
  E --> M
```

**Worked score:** `miss = np.linalg.norm(measured_landing_xy - predicted_landing_xy)` measures landing prediction error in meters; score bin hits separately from prediction accuracy.

## Common pitfalls

- **Fictitious torque mode:** STS3215 position-offset feedforward is not a native closed-loop torque interface; calibrate and bound the adapter rather than sending torque numbers as angles.
- **Overfitting misses:** Correcting every landing with an arbitrary offset can conceal wrong release timing or actuator dynamics; evaluate untouched trials.
- **Absent data:** Mark no-release events, missing landing measurements, and infeasible distances explicitly; do not manufacture a three-distance success claim.

> **Watch out:** Keep people outside the arm and projectile envelope; use a light foam ball and physical containment.

## When it's done

- **Artifact:** Publish slow-motion video, all attempted distances, hit/miss counts, predicted/measured landing plots, model revisions, tracking errors, and a clear account of unachieved goals.
